tldr: This paper introduces CoCoBench, a benchmark designed to diagnose coordination failures—such as redundant work and resource contention—that are often masked by standard overall success rates in multi-robot tasks. By breaking coordination down into four fundamental mechanisms and evaluating full trajectories, the benchmark tests 11 leading multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The results reveal that coordination capabilities are highly construct-specific: high overall success does not guarantee competence across different coordination patterns.
hero_caption: An illustration of the core motivation behind CoCoBench. When evaluating multi-agent coordination solely by final task success rates, benchmarks miss crucial coordination breakdowns such as serialized execution by a single robot, ordering violations, resource contention, and desynchronized handoffs. CoCoBench introduces trajectory-level construct scores to objectively evaluate not just whether the goal was met, but whether agents coordinated properly.
overview:
Using large language models and multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as the "brains" of embodied robots to perform complex multi-agent household chores has become an active area of research. However, existing benchmarks suffer from a major blind spot: they rely heavily on final task success rate. Under this metric, if a single robot serializes an entire job that was meant to be parallelized across the team, or if robots repeatedly fight over shared tools before finally reaching the goal, the run is still counted as a complete "success."

To address this gap, the authors developed CoCoBench, a benchmark that breaks household multi-robot coordination into four core mechanisms (constructs): task allocation, sequential ordering, mutual exclusion, and handoff coordination. Each construct can be evaluated independently and quantitatively. Built inside the AI2-THOR simulator across 897 executable instances, CoCoBench relies on a unified high-level skill interface. This design directly exposes high-level planning and coordination logic without being confounded by low-level motor execution errors.

Evaluating 11 leading MLLMs—spanning proprietary commercial APIs to open-weight models—revealed striking imbalances in coordination skills. Even GPT-5.6-sol, the top-performing model overall, was outperformed by open models on task allocation. Meanwhile, some models strictly obeyed coordination rules but timed out before completion. This study offers crucial insights into the true bottlenecks of embodied multi-agent robotics.
contributions: Formulating embodied multi-agent coordination planning as a trajectory-level coupling problem, clearly defining four recurring coordination constructs found in household tasks.

Constructing CoCoBench, an oracle-validated benchmark of 897 instances in AI2-THOR, and introducing trajectory-level Construct Scores (CS) that measure coordination quality independently of task success.

Evaluating 11 leading MLLMs across centralized vs. decentralized modes, communication setups, visual vs. blind inputs, and agent team sizes, uncovering structural bottlenecks in current multi-agent coordination planning.

sections.heading: Moving Beyond "Ends Justify the Means" Evaluation
sections.summary: In multi-robot environments powered by MLLMs, coordination failures like redundant work, ordering violations, and tool contention can occur even when visual perception and basic actions succeed. Because standard success rates hide these issues, the authors propose CoCoBench to directly diagnose the mechanisms of coordination.
sections.details:
Research using MLLMs as robot planners has advanced rapidly, shifting attention from single-agent tasks to collaborative team problems. Many household tasks, such as tidying up or meal preparation, are best solved when multiple robots divide the work.

However, a significant challenge remains: there has been no standardized benchmark to measure how well robots actually coordinate. Most existing benchmarks track only whether the final target state was achieved (Success Rate). Under this metric, severe coordination breakdowns receive top marks—for instance, when one agent does all the work while the other idles, when an agent shuts a cabinet too early and blocks a teammate, or when agents repeatedly fight over a single knife before finally finishing.

To solve this, the authors introduce CoCoBench, featuring 897 executable instances. It categorizes household coordination into four representative patterns: task allocation, sequential ordering, mutual exclusion, and handoff coordination. By computing a Construct Score (CS) alongside task success, CoCoBench distinguishes between "ends justify the means" planning and genuinely disciplined, efficient coordination.

captions.F3: An overview of the CoCoBench framework. It features a three-stage pipeline consisting of task design across four coordination dimensions, agent role assignment, and coupled execution via high-level skills, all implemented as executable household tasks in a simulator.

sections.heading: Blind Spots in Existing Benchmarks and CoCoBench's Niche
sections.summary: While embodied benchmarks have expanded from single-agent setups to multi-agent teams, none isolate and evaluate individual coordination mechanisms. CoCoBench significantly advances the field in both task diversity and coverage of coordination constructs.
sections.details:
Embodied agent research in household environments has progressed rapidly within simulators like AI2-THOR and Habitat. Early benchmarks such as ALFWorld targeted single agents and were not built to measure workload balancing or synchronization across multiple robots.

Recently, multi-agent benchmarks such as MECoBench, RoCoBench, and PARTNR have emerged. In particular, MECoBench incorporates parallel and sequential tasks. However, its instances mix multiple dependencies together, making it difficult to pinpoint the exact mechanistic failure mode when a coordination breakdown occurs.

CoCoBench's main advantage lies in formalizing coordination into four distinct, isolated dimensions, each evaluated with a dedicated trajectory-level score. This design cleanly separates failures in low-level motor execution from breakdowns in high-level multi-agent coordination logic.

captions.F2: Comparison with related embodied benchmarks. The horizontal axis indicates the coverage of coordination dimensions (Task allocation T, Sequential ordering S, Mutual exclusion M, and Handoff H), while the vertical axis shows task type diversity. CoCoBench (red star) covers all four dimensions, standing out in both task diversity and evaluation granularity.

sections.heading: Formulating Multi-Robot Coordination Mathematically
sections.summary: This work formalizes multi-agent coordination as a trajectory-level coupled planning problem over a fixed set of high-level skills. It focuses on "coordination coupling," where one agent's action alters another agent's feasibility or efficiency, and evaluates performance along two axes: success rate and construct score.
sections.details:
A task instance is defined by a household environment, a team of agents, a state space, an observation function, a fixed set of high-level skills, a shared executor, a goal predicate set, a step budget, and a target coordination construct.

At each step, agents select high-level skills based on their observation histories. The shared executor runs these actions and logs environment events such as precondition violations, resource contention, and idle waits. If all goal predicates are satisfied at the final step, the episode is marked successful (SR = 1).

The paper's core concept is "Coordination Coupling." This occurs when an action taken by agent $a_i$ alters the validity, cost, or feasibility of an action available to agent $a_j$. Typical examples include one robot closing a cabinet and preventing another from placing an item, or two robots competing for a single kitchen knife.

From the full trajectory $\tau$, CoCoBench computes both binary task success and a continuous Construct Score $C_d(\tau) \in [0, 1]$ measuring coordination quality. This formulation isolates team-level planning competence from confounding low-level manipulation failures.

sections.heading: Four Coordination Patterns and Rigorous Trajectory Scoring
sections.summary: The authors define four key coordination dimensions common in household tasks—task allocation, sequential ordering, mutual exclusion, and handoff—and design dedicated scoring functions for each. Instances generated in AI2-THOR are filtered through a strict three-tier verification gate.
sections.details:
The four coordination dimensions (D1 to D4) in CoCoBench and their scoring metrics are designed as follows:

- D1: Task Allocation
Covers parallelizable tidying tasks where the goal is balanced load distribution. The score compares actual makespan $M$ with the oracle makespan $M^*$ using $C_{\mathrm{D1}} = \max(0, 1 - (M - M^*)/M^*)$. Serializing the work on a single robot severely lowers this score.

- D2: Sequential Ordering
Covers tasks requiring strict causal ordering, such as opening a cabinet, having all agents place items, and then closing it. Factoring in precondition violations $v$ and illegal action flags $p_{\mathrm{legal}}$, it is scored as $C_{\mathrm{D2}} = p_{\mathrm{legal}} \cdot \max(0, 1 - v/n)$.

- D3: Mutual Exclusion
Covers scenarios where multiple agents share a single resource, such as one knife for meal preparation. Based on resource contention events $c$ and total execution steps $L$, it is evaluated via $C_{\mathrm{D3}} = \max(0, 1 - c/a) \cdot \min(1, M^*/L)$, penalizing contention and encouraging efficient handoffs.

- D4: Handoff Coordination
Covers relay tasks where items pass through an intermediate buffer table. Mismatches between producer and consumer paces cause buffer overflows ($o$) or empty waits ($w$). The metric penalizes both: $C_{\mathrm{D4}} = \max(0, 1 - (o + w)/h)$.

To construct high-quality instances, scenes generated from symbolic templates must pass three rigorous quality gates: an Arrangement Gate verifying spatial reachability, an Oracle Gate ensuring solvability by a privileged reference policy, and a Metric Gate confirming near-perfect oracle scores. Only 897 verified instances were retained.

captions.F4: Concrete execution examples across the four coordination dimensions. D1 illustrates parallel tidying, D2 shows strict adherence to cabinet opening/closing order, D3 depicts shared-knife contention avoidance, and D4 displays an item relay mediated by an intermediate buffer table.

sections.heading: Evaluating 11 Models Reveals Specific Strengths and Limits
sections.summary: Evaluating 11 commercial and open MLLMs showed that coordination skills are highly construct-specific. Removing visual input did not degrade performance, confirming that symbolic planning is the primary bottleneck. Furthermore, coordination performance dropped sharply as team size increased.
sections.details:
The experiments compared proprietary models like GPT-5.6-sol and Claude Opus 4.8 against open-weight models including RoboBrain2.5-8B and InternVL3.5-8B. Key findings include:

- Construct-Specific Strengths
While GPT-5.6-sol achieved the highest overall score (SR 84.8%, CS 0.90), Qwen3-VL-8B led in D1 (allocation), Claude Opus 4.8 led in D2 (ordering), and GPT-5.6-sol dominated in D3 and D4. Even the strongest overall models are not universally superior across all coordination types.

- Centralized vs. Decentralized and Communication
Centralized coordination (C0: SR 48.0%, CS 0.69), where a single model decides all actions from pooled states, substantially outperformed decentralized setups. Adding a shared communication channel improved decentralized performance (SR 39.6%, CS 0.65 vs. SR 36.7%, CS 0.63 without communication), but still lagged far behind the centralized approach.

- Symbolic Planning, Not Vision, Is the Bottleneck
When visual camera feeds were removed and agents received only text observations (history and available actions), overall success rate stayed flat—even ticking up slightly from 40.6% with images to 42.3% blind. This strongly indicates that high-level skill selection is bottlenecked by symbolic reasoning and role assignment rather than visual perception.

- Scalability Degrades with Team Size
Performance steadily decreased as team size expanded from 2 agents (SR 48.8%) to 3 (45.8%) and 4 (43.1%). Open-weight models suffered the steepest drops; for instance, InternVL3.5-8B fell from 16.9% with 2 agents down to 7.7% with 4 agents.

- Discrepancy Between Success Rate and Plan Validity
Claude Opus 4.8 generated valid, rule-abiding coordination plans in 96.3% of episodes, yet achieved an SR of only 78.5% due to cautious timeouts. Conversely, models like Claude Haiku 4.5 and Qwen3.6-Plus frequently cut corners or violated ordering rules to force task completion, proving that success rate alone misrepresents coordination health.

captions.F5: Pearson correlation matrix among the four construct scores computed from GPT-5.6-sol trajectories. All off-diagonal correlations fall between -0.10 and 0.16, confirming that the four coordination constructs measure distinct and mutually independent planning capabilities.

sections.heading: A Solid Step Toward Diagnosing Multi-Agent Robotics
sections.summary: CoCoBench decomposes multi-robot coordination into four foundational constructs, separating goal completion from the quality of the coordination process itself. It serves as an essential diagnostic tool for designing future multi-agent models and dedicated coordination architectures.
sections.details:
This study introduced CoCoBench, a benchmark providing fine-grained diagnostics for embodied multi-agent coordination planning in household tasks. Addressing the limitation of prior benchmarks where overall success rates obscure coordination failures, the authors established trajectory-level evaluation scores based on four core constructs: task allocation, sequential ordering, mutual exclusion, and handoff coordination.

Extensive experiments across 11 MLLMs quantitatively highlighted model-specific coordination profiles, the necessity of centralized state aggregation, fragility under larger team sizes, and the gap between success rate and plan validity. CoCoBench's code and dataset are released open source, providing a solid foundation for guiding the development of future cooperative multi-robot systems.

sections.heading: Appendix: Task Details and Failure Analysis
sections.summary: The appendix provides details on the 10 task families, prompt templates, and an in-depth breakdown of failure modes. Open models were predominantly hindered by protocol violations and step budget exhaustion, accompanied by an analysis of computational cost versus step efficiency.
sections.details:
The appendix supplements the main paper with experimental statistics and concrete task examples:

- Benchmark Composition
CoCoBench's 897 instances are evenly distributed across 10 task families spanning all four dimensions: D1 (Store Groceries, Sort & Store, Tidy Drawers), D2 (Stock Cabinet, Load in Order, Fill Drawers in Order), D3 (Prepare Food), and D4 (Relay Items, Indirect Relay, Cross-Zone Handoff).

- Failure Mode Decomposition
Analyzing failed episodes revealed that commercial models rarely violated protocols (averaging 1.0%), with budget timeouts being their primary cause of failure. In contrast, open models averaged 17.5% protocol violations. Budget timeouts accounted for 61% of failures in InternVL3.5-8B and 52% in RoboBrain2.5-8B, highlighting significant challenges in formatting compliance and search efficiency.

- Computational Cost vs. Efficiency
Looking at episode runtimes, GPT-5.6-sol achieved top performance with an average of 18.4 steps and 123.8 seconds. Claude Opus 4.8 took a similar number of steps but required 296.9 seconds. Open models often exceeded 30 steps, indicating that high-level indecision directly led to action inefficiencies.

captions.F10: A pie chart showing the distribution of the four coordination dimensions and ten task families in CoCoBench. The dimensions are balanced to ensure comprehensive, unbiased evaluation.

takeaways: Evaluating multi-robot coordination solely by task success rate is misleading; trajectory-level Construct Scores (CS) are necessary to capture protocol violations and inefficiencies.
Current state-of-the-art MLLMs exhibit uneven coordination profiles, often excelling in one coordination pattern (e.g., sequential ordering) while stumbling in another (e.g., mutual exclusion).
When low-level skills are abstracted away, planning performance is bottlenecked by symbolic reasoning and dynamic role assignment rather than visual perception.
Scaling to larger teams and decentralized execution causes steep performance drops, emphasizing the need for centralized reasoning mechanisms or more structured communication protocols.
limitations: Low-level motor control (such as navigation and manipulation failures) is handled by an idealized skill executor, omitting physical collisions and trajectory-level dynamic interference.
The benchmark relies on the AI2-THOR simulator, abstracting away real-world sensor noise, communication latency, and physical dynamic uncertainties.
A substantial gap in protocol following exists between open-weight and commercial models, leading many open models to fail before their true coordination logic can be fairly evaluated.
